title: Pre-shot routine: the same steps in the same order
summary: A short pre-shot routine helps you shoot the same way in training and in competition: six steps that fit the time limits of Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting.

body.html: A pre-shot routine is a fixed set of steps you repeat before each target. It helps you read the target, set up the same way and call only when you are ready.

Studies of routines in many sports show a small to moderate benefit, also under pressure. They were not done in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting, but most likely it works the same way here.
Under pressure many shooters change their tempo without noticing: they rush the call, or stand too long and check each detail twice. A familiar routine gives you something simple to do instead.

html: Feet: set your stance for the break point, the place where you plan to break the target.
Gun: take your start position with the muzzles at the hold point, where they wait for the call. In Sporting™ the gun starts down (see below).
Eyes: look at the pick-up point, where you first see the target clearly, with a soft focus: a calm, wide look.
Breath and cue: one natural breath out, shoulders down, then your cue word.
Call: give the call the same way each time and stay ready during the short delay before the target appears.
Target: switch to a hard focus on the target and keep your eyes on it through the shot.

html.sporting: Gun down: the heel of the stock touches your body, and the top of the stock stays below the line on your vest until the target is visible (Chapter 3 · Ready position: feet and gun). You have at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles (Chapter 7 · 15 seconds between targets). After your call the referee signals the trapper, and the target leaves within 3 seconds of the referee's signal (Chapter 5 · Calling for the target and the 3-second release).
html.compak: The gun position at the call is free: mounted or not (Chapter 17 · Gun position when calling). You have at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target (Chapter 21 · 10 seconds to call: warning, then penalty). The target leaves within 3 seconds of the call with a manual release, or half a second after it with a sonopull (voice release) (Chapter 2 · Releasing targets: manual, remote, sonopull).

body.html: Keep the order of the steps, not an exact number of seconds. The delay after the call can vary (in Sporting™, and in Compak® Sporting with a manual release), so the time can change a little. Stay well inside the limit: ask a coach or a friend to time your routine in training.
If something disturbs you before the call, such as a noise, a thought or the sun, do not call. Lower the gun, breathe out and start the routine again, within the time limit.
For a double, plan both targets before you call: where you break the first one, and where your eyes go for the second. Treat them as two separate shots.

Between stands, a longer routine helps you put the last stand behind you, whatever the score. Open the gun, take out the empty cases, drink some water and look at the next targets. In Compak® Sporting you change stations with the gun open and unloaded (Chapter 17 · 10 seconds to call; change stations with the gun open).
Load only on the stand, with the gun pointing down the range, once the referee has allowed shooting to start (Chapter 8 · When and how to load, Chapter 21 · When you may shoot and load).
Build the routine in training and keep it the same at competitions. Agree your plan with your coach before the event, so on the day you only need to follow it.
During a competition, nobody may coach a competitor (Chapter 8 · No coaching during competition, Chapter 21 · No coaching during competition).

notes.html: Stay silent while the shooter runs the routine. In training, translate between targets and briefly; in competition, pass on only the referee's decisions and official messages.
Time a new shooter's routine in training. If it does not fit the limit with a margin, cut steps rather than rushing them.

key_points.html: A routine is the same steps in the same order before each target.
Keep the order; the seconds may vary a little, as long as you stay inside the limit.

Sporting™: gun down and at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles. Compak® Sporting: free gun position and at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target.
Disturbed before the call? Lower the gun, breathe out and start again.
Build the routine in training: no coaching is allowed during a competition.

did_you_know.html: Shooters usually call “pull” or “ready”, the words named in the Sporting™ rules. Saying the call the same way each time helps, especially in Compak® Sporting, where a sonopull may release the target by voice.

quiz.q: What should stay the same in your routine from one target to the next?
quiz.explain: The order of the steps matters more than the seconds; the delay after the call can vary anyway (in Sporting™, and in Compak® Sporting with a manual release).

quiz.q: Where is the gun when you call in Sporting™?

options.text: Already mounted firmly at the shoulder
Anywhere: the gun position is free
Down, the stock below the vest line

quiz.explain: In Sporting™ the gun stays down until the target is visible. In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free.

quiz.q: A noise disturbs you before you call. What can you do?

options.text: Lower the gun, breathe out and start again
Call quickly, before the same noise comes back
Ask the referee to show the target again

quiz.explain: Until you call, you can restart your routine, as long as you stay within the time limit.
